I've been farming this land for 45 years. Quzhou is not easy — the summers are hot, winters dry, and we depend on the wells. My body isn't what it was, and my son works in the city, so I manage mostly with hired machines now. But I know this land, and I know what it needs.

**My reasoning:**

All 20 mu rotates. Wheat goes in after the maize comes out in late September/October, and maize goes in right after I harvest the wheat in June. That's how it's been my whole life here on the North China Plain. I don't split the area — I use all 20 mu for each crop sequentially.

For **wheat**, I'll plant an improved variety — I've used Jimai 22 for several years and the yields are steady and the lodging resistance is good. I apply base fertilizer before planting and topdress at jointing — that's the critical moment. Three irrigations: one before winter sets in, one at jointing, one at heading. I can't skip the jointing water, the soil gets too dry by March. Two pesticide passes — herbicide in winter, and a fungicide/aphid spray before heading. I do rotary tillage. Deep ploughing on my own is too hard now, and rotary gets the job done fine for wheat establishment.

For **maize**, I go straight into the wheat stubble with no-till seeding — saves me time and moisture. I use a popular hybrid, Zhengdan 958, which I've had consistent results with. Maize needs water at silking most critically. I'll irrigate twice — once around big flare stage, once at silking/grain fill — unless rainfall is good, but in Quzhou I don't count on it. Fertilizer goes in mostly as base, with a topdress at the 8-10 leaf stage. Two pesticide applications — one early for armyworm, one if needed later.

I'm not chasing maximum yields at 68. I want stable, reliable production with manageable labor.
